draft.title: Molar volume of gases
card: Equal amounts of any gas take up the same volume when the temperature and pressure are the same. So one mole of hydrogen and one mole of carbon dioxide fill the same space.
This volume is called the molar volume. At 25°C and 100 kPa it is 24.79 L/mol. At 0°C and 100 kPa it is 22.71 L/mol.
To find the volume of a gas, use V = n × 24.79. To find the moles, use n = V ÷ 24.79. Use these only when the gas is at 25°C and 100 kPa.
The molar volume does not depend on the type of gas or the size of its particles. It changes only if the temperature or pressure changes.
draft.remember: At the same temperature and pressure, one mole of any gas has the same volume.

a.q: At 25°C and 100 kPa, which sample has the same volume as 1.0 mol of oxygen gas?
a.why: At the same temperature and pressure, equal moles of any gas have equal volume, so 1.0 mol of helium matches. The 32 g of helium is about 8 mol, so it fills a much larger volume. Matching mass does not mean matching moles.
a.clue: Compare the number of moles, not the mass.

b.q: Mia collects carbon dioxide from a reaction in her school lab at 25°C and 100 kPa. The gas has a mass of 4.40 g (M = 44.0 g/mol). What volume does it occupy?
b.why: The moles are 4.40 ÷ 44.0 = 0.100 mol. The volume is 0.100 × 24.79 = 2.48 L. The answer of 24.8 L is tempting, but it is the volume of a full mole, not 0.100 mol.
b.clue: Find the moles from the mass first, then use the molar volume.

check.summary: No problems found. The molar volumes (24.79 L/mol at 25°C and 22.71 L/mol at 0°C, both at 100 kPa) match the NSW data sheet, and both answers and explanations check out.
